doc.title: Dave Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Wilton, Connecticut, November 21, 2001

title: Bach Partita commission, 'Regret' for Pieta, and masses in Europe
summary: Brubeck describes writing a Bourree for Simon Blendis's Bach project, 'Regret' for the Canadian group Pieta, and applause for his mass in Vienna, Munich and Berlin.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: And then just before that a solo violinist named Simon Blendis, B-L-E-N-D-I-S, said he’s taking Bach “Partita” and it’s I think six movements, and he’s asking six composers to write a section after each composer. And again I’m thinking oh I don’t want to get involved in this. And I did it. And he’s played it. I went to the performance. All six composers were in London and we all had to go on stage. But I did the Bouree. And the Gigue I think was the last movement and I loved what the composer did with that. I liked mine, but I liked his better. And he’s an Irish composer and he got into Irish jig fiddle stuff, and it really worked. It was just a natural. But these are the kinds of things — now that’ll probably be recorded this year. Then a group called Pieta, after the Palestrina orphan girls, you remember that?

Orphan girls. And he made such great musicians out of them that they were always called on and it supported the orphanage. And great music was written for those girls. And they became great musicians. So there’s a group in Canada, all girls, all women, and they asked me to write them a piece. And they call themselves Pieta. And they were going to be performing at the Montreal Jazz Festival, and would I write a piece. So that’s a recent piece and it’s called “Regret.” A very sad piece. And just for all strings, but it will work for string quartet too. It will work for just one of each. And they played it live at the festival and the jazz audience loved it. The year before we did our mass at the jazz festival and had a standing ovation. We just did a mass in Vienna, Munich and East Berlin and I was afraid, in English, to do a mass in these countries that are so revered for music. They applauded “The Lord’s Prayer.” They applauded all the way through this piece. And got three standing ovations in one country in the middle of the mass.
